questions.question: Bright Ltd. is planning to expand its production capacity. For expansion, it requires an additional ₹10,00,000. The management is considering financing the expansion through either equity shares or debt. At the present level of operations, the company has an EBIT of ₹8,00,000. The company is considering issuing 10% debentures of ₹10,00,000. After expansion, EBIT is expected to increase by 25%. Calculate the Financial Leverage after expansion. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Bright Ltd. – Financial leverage after expansion
  • Existing EBIT = 8, 00,000;
  • Expected increase = 25%;
  • Additional debentures = 10, 00,000 at 10%.
  • Increase in EBIT = 8, 00,000 × 25% = 2, 00,000
  • EBIT after expansion = 8, 00,000 + 2, 00,000 = 10, 00,000
  • Interest = 10, 00,000 × 10% = 1, 00,000
  • EBT = EBIT − Interest = 10, 00,000 − 1, 00,000 = 9, 00,000
  • Financial leverage = EBIT / EBT = 10, 00,000 / 9, 00,000 = 1.11 times
  • Financial leverage after expansion is approximately 1.11 times, using the simple EBIT/EBT

questions.question: What is Profitability Index method? How is this method superior to NPV method? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Profitability Index and comparison with NPV
  • The Profitability Index (PI), also known as the benefit–cost ratio, measures the present value of
  • future cash inflows per rupee invested.
  • PI = Present value of cash inflows / Initial investment
  • Decision rule
  • PI Decision
  • > 1 Accept, subject to other constraints
  • = 1 Financially indifferent; NPV = 0
  • < 1 Reject at the specified discount rate
  • How PI can be useful compared with NPV
  • • Relative profitability: PI shows present value generated per rupee invested; NPV shows
  • absolute value added.
  • • Capital rationing: PI can help compare relative attractiveness when investment funds are
  • limited.
  • • Ranking: PI provides a convenient ratio for ranking independent projects when ratio ranking is
  • appropriate.
  • • Time value of money: like NPV, PI discounts future cash flows.
  • • Cash-flow basis: PI uses discounted cash flows rather than accounting profit.
  • 26900132
  • MG5DSCCOM302
  • PI is useful for assessing investment efficiency and capital rationing, while NPV remains a
  • fundamental value-maximising criterion.

questions.question: A company is considering two projects. Project A requires ₹4,00,000 and has an average annual profit of ₹80,000. Project B requires ₹5,00,000 and has an average annual profit of ₹1,25,000. Calculate ARR and select the better project. / [CO4] [7x4 = 28]
questions.solution_html:
• Calculate ARR and select the better project
  • ARR measures average annual accounting profit as a percentage of investment. As the question
  • provides only initial investment and does not give useful life or residual value, the initial-investment
  • denominator is used.
  • ARR = (Average annual profit / Initial investment) × 100
  • Project A
  • ARR = (₹80,000 / ₹4,00,000) × 100 = 20%
  • Project B
  • ARR = (₹1,25,000 / ₹5,00,000) × 100 = 25%
  • Particulars Project A Project B
  • Initial investment ₹4,00,000 ₹5,00,000
  • Average annual profit ₹80,000 ₹1,25,000
  • ARR 20% 25%
  • Selection: Project B is preferable under the ARR criterion because it provides a higher accounting
  • return of 25%, compared with 20% for Project A.
  • Mark allocation: Formula (1); Project A calculation (2); Project B calculation (2); comparison and
  • selection (2).

questions.question: What is Optimum capital structure? Explain the features of Optimum capital structure. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• What is optimum capital structure? Explain its features.
  • Capital structure refers to the composition of long-term sources of finance used by a company,
  • generally including equity share capital, preference share capital, retained earnings and long-term debt.
  • Optimum capital structure is the combination of debt and equity financing that minimizes the
  • overall cost of capital and maximizes the value of the firm, subject to relevant assumptions and risks.
  • Features
  • • Minimum overall cost of capital: It achieves the lowest feasible weighted average cost of
  • capital for the firm.
  • • Maximum firm value: It supports maximisation of total market value; lower financing costs
  • may increase the present value of future cash flows.
  • • Proper balance between debt and equity: It balances borrowed funds and owners' funds.
  • Excessive debt increases financial risk, while excessive equity may be relatively expensive.
  • • Reasonable financial risk: It avoids an unsustainable debt burden and helps preserve the
  • ability to service obligations.
  • • Benefit from financial leverage: Debt can improve equity earnings when business returns
  • exceed the relevant cost of debt, but it can also magnify losses.
  • • Flexibility: It preserves the ability to raise additional funds for expansion and unexpected
  • needs.
  • 26900132
  • MG5DSCCOM302
  • • Solvency and liquidity: It maintains the capacity to meet commitments and avoids excessive
  • default risk.
  • • Control considerations: Equity can dilute voting control; debt usually has no equivalent
  • voting rights, though lenders may impose covenants.
  • • Tax advantages of debt: Interest is generally deductible for corporate tax purposes subject to
  • applicable rules, which may reduce the effective cost of debt.
  • • Business risk: Firms with unstable earnings generally have less capacity to support high fixed
  • interest commitments.
  • • Creditworthiness and market conditions: Interest rates, investor expectations, credit ratings
  • and financial position affect the cost and availability of finance.
  • • Compatibility with long-term objectives: The structure should support growth, investment,
  • dividend policy and overall strategy.
  • Optimum capital structure is not simply the structure with the highest debt or lowest equity. It is
  • the financing mix that balances cost, risk, control, flexibility and solvency while supporting firm-value
  • maximization.
